hero.name: Girish
hero.who: a hardware shop owner in Hubballi unsure whose advice to trust with his savings

story.b: Girish has run his hardware shop near the old market for twenty-two years. Now he has eight lakh rupees saved, and everyone has advice. A man in a share-tips group says a small company will double by Diwali. His brother-in-law swears by a land plot near the new bypass. A smooth young agent at the bank pushes a policy with a glossy brochure. Each sounds confident. Each says Girish would be foolish to miss out. Late one night, counting the day's cash, Girish realises he cannot tell who is right. He only knows that this money took him twenty years to build, and none of them would lose a rupee if it vanished.

ask.q: Girish is flooded with confident advice about his savings. What question should he ask first?
o: Which adviser sounds the most confident and successful?
Which option promises the highest return the fastest?
What does each adviser lose if their advice goes wrong?
ask.why: Confidence costs nothing, and high promised returns usually hide high risk. Asking what each adviser loses if things go wrong shows whose judgment has real weight behind it. Advice from someone who shares the pain is far more careful than advice from someone who only shares the talk.

chapters.take: Before trusting advice, ask who pays if it goes wrong.

story.h: The pump he would not use
story.b: A distributor offers Girish a fat margin on a new brand of water pump. Farmers who come into the shop trust his word completely. Selling it would be easy. Then a farmer from Kundgol asks a simple question. Would Girish put this pump on his own borewell? Girish hesitates. The honest answer is no. He does not know the brand yet. That night he makes a rule for the shop. He will only push products he would use himself, and for new brands he will give his own replacement promise for six months. He installs one of the new pumps at his own house first. If it fails, he wants to be the first to feel it.

ask.q: Girish's son Kiran wants the shop to start selling a cheap new brand of tiles. How should they decide whether to recommend it?
o: Recommend it, since customers make their own choices anyway
Use it in their own home or back it with their own guarantee first
Push it hard, because the margin is too good to miss
ask.why: When the person recommending something also carries its risk, they become far more careful. Using the tiles at home or backing them personally puts the family's own risk behind the advice. Leaving it all to customers, or chasing the margin, hands the downside to people who trusted them.

chapters.take: Good decisions come from people who carry the downside of them.

story.b: Girish starts asking each adviser one quiet question. Do you own this yourself? The man in the share-tips group goes silent, then says he only shares research. The bank agent admits, when pressed, that his commission on the policy is large and paid upfront. His brother-in-law has never bought any land near the bypass himself, though he talks about it at every family function. Girish notices that the louder the advice, the less the adviser seemed to have at stake. Then he thinks of his old friend Mahesh, a retired schoolteacher, who quietly invests a little each month and talks about it only when asked.

ask.q: A relative strongly pushes a policy, and Girish learns he earns a commission on it. How should Girish treat the advice?
o: Weigh it carefully, knowing the relative gains even if the policy does not suit him
Trust it fully, since family would never mislead him
Reject it instantly, since anyone earning commission must be lying
ask.why: A commission does not make advice false, but it gives the adviser a reason to push regardless of fit. Knowing that, Girish can check the policy on its own merits. Blind trust ignores the hidden interest, and instant rejection throws away information that might still be useful.

chapters.take: Judge advice by what the adviser risks, not by how sure they sound.

story.h: The contractor who would not budge
story.b: Looking at his shelves one slow afternoon, Girish notices something odd. Five years ago he stocked three grades of PVC pipe. Now he stocks only the costlier certified kind. How did that happen? He traces it back to one contractor, Basavaraj, who refused to buy anything else and would walk out if offered cheaper pipes. Most other customers did not mind either way, as long as the price was fair. Keeping two kinds was a bother, so slowly the shop just followed Basavaraj. One stubborn man had quietly set the rule for everyone. Girish laughs. Then he wonders where else in the market the same thing has happened.

ask.q: Girish's wife Shobha wants the colony's sports day lunch to be plastic-free. Most families do not mind either way. What is her best move?
o: Wait for a majority vote, since rules need most people's support
Get a few families to firmly refuse plastic, since the others will go along
Convince every single family one by one before changing anything
ask.why: When most people are flexible and a few are firm, the firm few often set the rule. A handful of families who will not use plastic makes plastic-free the easy choice for everyone. A vote lets indifference decide, and convincing every family takes months the lunch does not have.

chapters.take: A small, firm group can set the rules for a flexible majority.

story.b: His brother-in-law has a new plan. Put all eight lakhs into the bypass land, then take a loan against the shop for a second plot. Land always goes up, he says, and in five years Girish will be rich. Girish thinks about it seriously. It might even work most of the time. But he pictures the other time. A delayed highway, a title dispute, a bad year at the shop, and the loan payments still due. He would lose the shop his father started. However good the usual outcome looks, that one bad case would end the game. So he draws a line. The shop and the house are never on the table.

ask.q: Kiran wants to put his whole first salary into a risky trading app. What advice fits best?
o: Go all in while he is young, since big risks bring big rewards
Borrow from friends to invest more, since the returns will cover it
Build an emergency fund first, and risk only what he could afford to lose
ask.why: The first rule is to avoid any loss that knocks you out completely. An emergency fund and small, affordable risks keep Kiran in the game for decades, which is where growth happens. Going all in or borrowing can win for a while, then one bad turn wipes him out.

chapters.take: Avoid ruin first. Staying in the game lets time work for you.

story.b: The shop needs rewiring. A new company with a slick app quotes a low price and promises smart switches. Ramesh, the old electrician two lanes away, has no app and no website. But half the shops in the market have used him for thirty years, and he still answers his phone at night. If his work fails, the whole market will know by evening. Girish picks Ramesh. He applies the same test to his savings. Instead of shiny new schemes, he talks to Mahesh, who has quietly invested for twenty years, and chooses plain, long-tested options: a fixed deposit for emergencies and a simple monthly SIP, after reading the fine print himself.

ask.q: Kiran wants to learn how to run a business. Whose guidance should he trust most?
o: A family friend who has run a profitable shop for twenty years
An online coach selling courses who has never run a business
A brand-new theory that claims all older methods are finished
ask.why: Someone whose own money and name have been tested by real customers for years has earned trust. The online coach is judged by course sales, not results, and a brand-new theory has not survived time yet. People and ideas that have lasted through hard years usually have something real behind them.

chapters.take: Trust people whose name is on the line and ideas that have survived time.

story.h: A quiet year at the shop
story.b: A year later, Girish's savings have not doubled, and nobody at the tea stall calls him clever. But the money is safe and growing slowly. The emergency fund covered three bad months when road work blocked the market. The share-tips group has gone quiet since its favourite company crashed. The bypass land is stuck in a legal dispute, and his brother-in-law no longer brings it up. The new pump at Girish's house still runs well, so he now recommends it with confidence, and farmers trust him even more. Kiran works at the shop on Saturdays. When a customer asks Girish for advice, he first tells them what he himself owns.

chapters.take: Trust grows where advice comes with real risk behind it.
